The BER of chipless RFID systems is mainly determined by the Radar Cross Section (RCS) of the tag.
Periodic arrangement of resonators in a fixed tag area can increase cross-polar RCS by up to 15 dB compared to non-periodic arrangements.
The RCS of a chipless tag is approximated as the product of the RCS of a metallic plate of the same area and the square of the tag's reflection coefficient.
Each resonator in the tag is modeled as a discrete scatterer with a specific complex reflection coefficient (amplitude and phase).
The received signal includes contributions from the tag, antenna coupling, clutter, and noise; clutter dominates over noise in typical indoor environments.
Clutter is modeled as a complex normal random process with average amplitude around -53 dB and standard deviation 2.3 dB.
Miniaturizing the tag reduces its RCS and thus increases BER, potentially degrading detection reliability.
The proposed semi-analytic method for RCS computation is significantly faster than full-wave solvers, reducing computation time from ~25 hours to seconds.
Mutual coupling among resonators is higher in periodic arrays but contributes to higher overall RCS and better BER performance.
Non-periodic resonator arrangements cause incoherent scattering, reducing the mono-static RCS and increasing BER.
Cross-polar RCS is important for polarization conversion, which improves tag detection.
Randomizing dipole positions inside the tag can reduce mutual coupling but generally lowers the maximum achievable RCS.
The bit sequence is correctly detected only if the useful backscattered signal exceeds the clutter and noise floor.
The tag's RCS depends on the operating wavelength, physical area, and reflection coefficient of the resonators.
The paper experimentally validates theoretical findings by measuring RCS and BER of fabricated chipless RFID tags.
The reflection coefficient maps show that periodic configurations have uniform amplitude and phase across resonators, unlike aperiodic ones.
The chipless RFID system is modeled as a radar communication system where the tag acts as a scatterer.
The paper uses array theory and physical optics combined with the Periodic Method of Moments (PMM) for efficient RCS computation.
The BER is a more meaningful figure of merit than bit/cm² or bit/Hz because it reflects decoding reliability.
The tag can be designed to maximize cross-polar scattering by selecting resonators with specific polarization conversion properties.
